title: Introducing State Rise: From Ashes
preview: An introduction to the studio and a grand strategy project about building a state from scratch.
content:
Greetings!

We are The Statecraft Bureau, an indie studio currently developing the grand strategy project State Rise: From Ashes — a game about building and developing a state from the ground up in the harsh world of the 20th century.

This is not just a city builder or an economic simulator. State Rise is a deep state management simulation where the player starts with an empty territory, a limited budget, and basic infrastructure. Over time, opportunities emerge for developing industry, logistics, foreign trade, population management, diplomacy, and military campaigns.

Inspired by projects such as Workers & Resources, Victoria, and Kaiserpunk, we aim to combine their strongest aspects while expanding the depth of gameplay. The core focus is state management on every level — from local decisions to influencing the global political stage.

Key Features

  • Complete start from scratch with manual infrastructure planning;
  • Complex production chains and an advanced economy;
  • Multi-layered logistics: from railways to retail distribution;
  • Foreign trade, diplomacy, and pressure from major powers;
  • Gradual scaling from a settlement to a fully developed state;
  • Adaptive complexity aimed both at thoughtful players who enjoy micromanagement and more casual audiences.

At the current stage, several major development milestones have already been completed: internal politics, diplomacy and international trade systems, the foundation of the economy and production chains, as well as city-building mechanics. Work is currently focused on transportation and logistics, including route optimization and cargo behavior systems.

The next major stage will be military campaigns, after which development focus will shift toward state AI and balancing technological progression.

The project is being developed without external funding or a marketing budget. The main resources behind it are time and consistent work. If the project interests you, you can support it through subscriptions, sharing, or feedback.

title: Game Start: The Birth of a State
preview: How a campaign begins and what challenges await the player during the first days.
content:
Greetings!

This is The Statecraft Bureau, and today we would like to take a closer look at the beginning of the game: how a state is born, where the player’s journey starts, and what systemic challenges appear during the very first in-game days.

In the standard scenario, the player truly begins from scratch: there are no buildings, no vehicles, and no population. The only things available are a limited budget, border checkpoints, and a territory waiting to be developed from the ground up. дальнейший progress depends entirely on your decisions regarding planning, construction, and resource distribution.

One of the key differences from many strategy games is the absence of instant construction. Every building is constructed through a contract-based system: you must organize construction offices, establish resource supply lines, and provide machinery. Even basic infrastructure requires time, logistics, and careful planning.

The population is not represented by abstract numbers, but by a full simulation of residents. Every person has their own needs and behavioral patterns: they require housing, food, goods, and services, go to work, and spend time resting. If the system fails to provide basic conditions, the population begins to lose efficiency or leave the state entirely.

Needs System

One of the core mechanics is the daily needs system. Every resident generates a daily demand for goods and services, which must be fulfilled through the city’s infrastructure. In addition:

  • Needs depend on the state’s development level and external factors;
  • The chosen ideology influences them (this mechanic is currently in development and will expand further in the future);
  • The degree of satisfaction directly affects productivity and social stability.

As a result, economy, logistics, and social policy become parts of one interconnected system.

Already Implemented

  • A complete “start from scratch” with manual infrastructure deployment;
  • A construction system based on contracts, logistics, and machinery;
  • Basic population simulation and life cycle systems;
  • A needs system that takes time of day into account;
  • A set of buildings including residential housing, warehouses, stores, industrial and service facilities.

These mechanics form the foundation of the gameplay and are already integrated with the economy, trade, and city-building systems implemented in previous development stages.

The project is being developed step by step. Versions up to v0.4 have already been completed, covering internal politics, diplomacy, economy, and construction. v0.5 — transportation and logistics is currently in active development, with the main focus on route optimization, resource flow distribution, and system scalability.

After that, development will move toward military campaigns, state AI, and the introduction of ideologies that will significantly influence population behavior and development strategies.

title: Urbanization and Settlement Development
preview: How city structure is formed and why every building affects quality of life.
content:
Greetings!

This is The Statecraft Bureau. In this entry, we will examine what makes a city more than just a collection of buildings and turns it into a fully functioning system.

In State Rise: From Ashes, settlement development is not linear expansion, but the result of strategic decisions made by the player. You begin with an empty territory and gradually shape the structure of your city: defining residential districts, placing industry, planning infrastructure, and integrating public spaces.

Zoning plays a key role. Mistakes made during the early stages — such as poorly placed industry or a lack of service buildings — directly affect logistics efficiency and the population’s quality of life.

Public Institutions

A city cannot develop through economy alone. Social infrastructure — schools, medical institutions, sports facilities, and cultural centers — forms the foundation of a stable system. These institutions influence:

  • population satisfaction;
  • labor productivity;
  • long-term development stability.

Ignoring these aspects can lead to the degradation of a settlement even when the economy is strong.

Urbanization System

One of the core mechanics is the urbanization points system. Every building contributes to the overall development level of a settlement, shaping its status — from a small village to a major city.

This level directly affects population expectations:

  • during the early stages, basic conditions such as housing, food, and minimal infrastructure are sufficient;
  • as the settlement grows, demands for education, healthcare, transportation, and leisure appear;
  • certain buildings can significantly increase the overall level and, as a result, raise the expectations of residents.

As a result, city growth requires balance: accelerating development also increases the complexity of managing the system.

Current Implementation

  • Urbanization points and settlement level systems;
  • The influence of buildings on development and population expectations;
  • Basic mechanics for public institutions;
  • Planning tools and phased city expansion systems.

These mechanics are already integrated with the economy and the core population simulation introduced in previous versions and will continue to expand as development progresses.

During the current development stage (v0.5 — transportation and logistics), special attention is being given to district connectivity: accessibility of facilities, travel times, and the efficiency of resource distribution between zones.

In the future, the urbanization system will be expanded with the influence of ideology, politics, and media, increasing the differences between state types and gameplay styles.

In the next entry, we will take a closer look at the population: needs structure, citizen behavior, and their role in the economy.

Follow the project’s development — many more systems and tools for deep strategic gameplay are still ahead.

title: Population: Work, Education, and Needs
preview: How society develops in the late game and why logistics and education become critical.
content:
Greetings!

This is The Statecraft Bureau. In previous publications, we covered the beginning of the game and the development of cities, but the key element of any system is its population. In State Rise: From Ashes, citizens are not abstract statistics, but the foundation of the entire economy and state management system.

Every individual goes through a complete life cycle: from birth to becoming part of the economy. During the early stages, this includes kindergartens and schools, followed by educational choices such as vocational education or university studies. The qualifications obtained directly determine a citizen’s role within the system.

Different groups of specialists influence the efficiency of various sectors:

  • technical specialists improve industrial productivity;
  • scientists accelerate research and technological development (this system will be expanded further with the technology tree update);
  • medical workers maintain the stability of the healthcare system.

As a result, education becomes a strategic resource rather than a secondary mechanic.

Transportation and Movement

An important part of the simulation is the physical movement of the population. Workers and students do not “teleport” to their destinations — they use the transportation system:

  • traveling to workplaces and educational institutions;
  • returning home afterward;
  • depending on route accessibility and infrastructure quality.

This creates an additional layer of complexity: players must account for transportation load, avoid congestion at key hubs, and properly organize residential and industrial zones. Within the current v0.5 version, logistics and route systems are actively being refined to ensure scalability as the population grows.

Needs and System Balance

Needs remain one of the core factors of stability. In the late game, they become significantly more complex and diverse:

  • basic needs: food, housing, healthcare;
  • infrastructure-related needs: transportation and access to services;
  • social needs: education, culture, and leisure.

As urbanization levels increase, expectations rise as well, and planning mistakes begin to have systemic consequences. Tens of thousands of citizens place pressure on both the economy and logistics, making management efficiency a critical factor.

Failure to satisfy needs leads to reduced productivity, worsening public mood, and potential destabilization of the state.

Future Expansion of the System

Future updates will significantly deepen the population simulation:

  • indirect needs will appear (security, access to information, media influence);
  • ideology will influence citizen expectations and behavior;
  • interaction with state institutions will expand (law enforcement and administrative structures are planned for v0.6–v0.9).

These additions will strengthen the connection between politics, economy, and social systems, making state management even more complex.

State Rise is not simply about constructing infrastructure. It is about simulating a society where every decision affects people’s lives and the long-term stability of the state.

You are not just building structures — you are shaping the system in which society develops.

title: Resources as the Foundation of the Economy
preview: The physical resource model, extraction systems, and the influence of logistics on state stability.
content:
Greetings!

This is The Statecraft Bureau. After discussing cities and population systems, we now move to the foundation of the entire simulation — resources and the economy.

In State Rise: From Ashes, the economy does not exist in abstract menus or spreadsheets, but directly on the map itself. The game already features more than 50 types of resources — from agricultural products to advanced industrial machinery. Every resource physically exists within the world: it is stored in warehouses or tanks, transported through logistics networks, and forms real supply flows.

This means that every operation — extraction, processing, or delivery — is tied to infrastructure and can create bottlenecks such as queues, congestion, and delays.

Resource Extraction

Natural resources are extracted from procedurally generated deposits. These include:

  • coal, oil, and natural gas;
  • iron and copper ore;
  • bauxite and other raw materials.

Although deposits do not become depleted during a single campaign, the main limitations come from distance, infrastructure accessibility, transportation capacity, and technological development.

As a result, the player’s primary challenge is not simply extraction, but building an efficient supply system and integrating resources into the broader economy.

Production Chains

Every resource is part of a production chain. Raw materials are processed, combined, and transformed into more advanced goods. These chains form industrial clusters, which become the core of the state economy.

At the current development stage (v0.3–v0.4), the foundational production chain system has already been implemented and integrated with logistics and construction mechanics. In the future, it will be expanded further with technological progression and regional specialization systems.

Resource Types and Transportation

Resources differ based on their physical characteristics:

  • bulk materials;
  • liquids and gases;
  • perishable goods;
  • industrial products.

Each category requires specialized transportation and infrastructure. Universal solutions do not exist: the player must design logistics networks while considering cargo characteristics, route layouts, and transportation scale.

As part of the ongoing development of v0.5, special attention is being paid to route optimization, flow distribution, and reducing congestion at transportation hubs.

Importance for Gameplay

Economic stability depends on balancing extraction, processing, and consumption. Disrupting this balance creates systemic problems:

  • resource shortages and halted production;
  • construction delays and infrastructure failures;
  • reduced efficiency across the entire economy.

Resources directly influence the pace of state development, the ability to engage in foreign trade, and participation in international politics.

Without a stable economy, it becomes impossible to maintain either social stability or military campaigns — every system in the game is interconnected.

title: Logistics and Transportation: The Connecting System of the Economy
preview: Modular vehicles, supply offices, and the management of resource flows.
content:
Greetings!

This is The Statecraft Bureau. If resources form the foundation of the economy, then logistics and transportation determine whether that economy can function effectively. They are what connect extraction, production, and consumption into a unified system.

In State Rise: From Ashes, transportation is not a secondary mechanic, but one of the core gameplay systems directly affecting the efficiency of the state.

Modular Transportation

Vehicles in the game are designed using a modular system. The player starts with a limited set of base vehicle types (eight categories in total), but can later create custom configurations tailored for specific purposes.

  • every type of cargo requires specialized transportation;
  • modules determine capacity, purpose, and efficiency;
  • there are no universal solutions — logistics chains must be adapted to specific tasks.

Vehicle design becomes part of the economy itself: transportation can be produced in industrial facilities and used either internally or exported through foreign trade.

This creates an additional strategic layer: decisions regarding industry and exports may have long-term consequences, including the possibility of other states using vehicles designed by the player.

Supply Offices

As the state grows, manually managing every route becomes inefficient. To address this, the game includes a supply office system:

  • the player defines the needs of a facility;
  • the system automatically distributes available vehicles;
  • routes are generated based on resource availability and priorities.

This reduces micromanagement and allows the player to focus on strategic decisions, especially during the later stages of the game.

Industrial Complexes

Buildings can be merged into unified industrial complexes. Instead of controlling every individual structure, the player manages an integrated production system:

  • mines, processing plants, and warehouses become part of a single network;
  • internal connections operate directly without relying on external logistics;
  • management overhead is reduced while production efficiency increases.

This architecture allows the economy to scale without causing exponential growth in management complexity.

Logistics as a Systemic Challenge

The transportation system takes real limitations into account:

  • road and infrastructure capacity;
  • route congestion and traffic formation;
  • industrial dependence on timely deliveries.

Planning mistakes create chain reactions: idle factories, resource shortages, and reduced economic efficiency.

Within the current v0.5 development stage, the main focus is route optimization, delivery stability, and ensuring scalability as population and economic complexity increase.

Importance for Strategy

Logistics determines the pace of state development. Even with abundant resources and industrial capacity, the absence of an effective transportation system makes the economy unstable.

The player effectively manages flows: identifying bottlenecks, deciding where infrastructure expansion is needed, and determining where route optimization is required.

Strong logistics form the foundation for every other system: economy, foreign trade, military campaigns, and political influence.

title: Economy and Production Chains
preview: How the state economy is formed and why production chains define the entire gameplay.
content:
Greetings!

This is The Statecraft Bureau. Today we will take a closer look at the economy — the system that connects all other mechanics in State Rise: From Ashes.

The economy in the game is built directly on the map itself: through resource extraction, processing, transportation, and final consumption. This is not an abstract model, but a physical system already integrated with logistics, population simulation, and city-building mechanics.

Production Chains

At the current stage, the game already includes around 70 types of industrial buildings, covering the entire process from raw resource extraction to the production of advanced machinery.

  • early stages: farms, sawmills, and basic processing facilities;
  • mid-game: factories and resource processing industries;
  • late game: heavy industry and machine-building complexes.

Many buildings also have smaller-scale variants, allowing the player to gradually expand the economy and adapt it to available resources and the scale of the state.

Players can choose between different development strategies:

  • an agricultural economy with distributed settlements;
  • an industrial model with concentrated production zones;
  • hybrid systems with regional specialization.

All production chains are tightly connected to transportation systems: without stable logistics, even advanced industry becomes inefficient.

Connection with Urbanization

The economy directly influences settlement development through the urbanization system:

  • small enterprises are suitable for early stages and local economies;
  • large industrial complexes form the foundation of the late game;
  • every building affects settlement level and population demands.

As a result, choosing the scale of production becomes a strategic decision: accelerating growth simultaneously increases the complexity of managing logistics and population needs.

System Integration

The economy is already connected to the project’s core mechanics:

  • logistics determine the efficiency of production chains (with v0.5 currently in active development);
  • the population provides workforce and generates demand;
  • foreign trade helps compensate shortages and encourages specialization.

This interconnection makes every decision meaningful: changes in one system inevitably affect the others.

Future: Management Automation

Future development stages will introduce a basic state AI system (v0.7), which players will be able to use for managing individual regions through administrative buildings.

The player will be able to delegate:

  • construction and infrastructure development;
  • logistics and supply management;
  • maintenance of regional economic stability.

This is especially important for the late game, where the scale of the state requires reducing micromanagement.

Importance for Gameplay

The economy is the core of State Rise. It determines:

  • the pace of state development;
  • resilience to crises;
  • foreign trade and diplomatic capabilities;
  • potential for military campaigns.

Well-designed production chains form the foundation of the entire system. Without them, neither stable development nor influence on the global stage is possible.

In future entries, we will continue exploring the project’s core systems and how they interact within a unified state simulation.

title: Construction System
preview: How construction works and why it requires logistics, resources, and planning.
content:
Greetings!

This is The Statecraft Bureau. Today we will examine one of the core systems of State Rise: From Ashes — construction.

In the game, construction is not an instant action, but a full process tightly connected to the economy, logistics, and population systems. Every building goes through the entire path from planning to completion, requiring resources, workforce, and proper organization.

Unique Projects

Every structure has its own requirements:

  • an individual set of resources;
  • different amounts of labor effort;
  • dependence on the complexity and purpose of the structure.

This makes construction varied and directly ties it to the current state of the economy.

Resources and Logistics

Building construction requires at least 11 types of resources, including construction materials, industrial products, and equipment.

  • all resources are physically transported through the logistics network;
  • specialized trucks are used depending on cargo type;
  • construction speed depends on supply stability.

As a result, construction becomes part of the larger logistics system. Supply disruptions directly slow down infrastructure development.

Workforce

Construction progress depends not only on resources, but also on labor:

  • workers contribute through labor-days;
  • they can arrive on foot or through transportation systems;
  • foreign workers can be employed through border checkpoints.

This ties construction to both population and transportation systems: without access to workforce, even a fully supplied construction site will stop functioning.

Integration with Other Systems

Construction is already integrated with the project’s core mechanics:

  • the economy provides materials and equipment;
  • logistics handle deliveries and routes;
  • the population forms the available workforce.

Failures in any of these systems result in delays and inefficiency.

Flexible Settings

To support different playstyles, the game includes a simplified mode:

  • resources and workforce are considered conditionally available;
  • costs are deducted directly from the budget;
  • construction happens instantly.

This mode allows players to focus on strategic aspects without deep logistical management.

Importance for Gameplay

The construction system makes every building part of a living economy. The player does not simply place structures, but organizes processes:

  • planning resource deliveries;
  • organizing workforce;
  • considering the impact on the transportation network.

This increases strategic depth: state development begins not with pre-built solutions, but with the gradual creation of infrastructure.

In the future, the system will be expanded further through integration with administrative structures and management automation, allowing players to handle large-scale construction projects more efficiently during the late game.

title: Foreign Trade and Economic Influence
preview: How trade works, why diplomacy matters, and why the economy extends beyond state borders.
content:
Greetings!

This is The Statecraft Bureau. Today we will take a detailed look at the foreign trade system — one of the key tools for state development in State Rise: From Ashes.

While the domestic economy forms the foundation, foreign trade allows the player to scale development, compensate for shortages, and strengthen influence on the global stage.

Customs and Physical Trade

Interaction with other states takes place through border crossings and customs offices. These are not abstract transactions:

  • resources are first purchased through diplomatic agreements;
  • afterward, they arrive at customs warehouses;
  • delivery deeper into the country is handled through the transportation system.

In the current version, the system is already integrated with logistics, while the development of v0.5 further increases the importance of route management and border throughput capacity. In the future, full simulation of deliveries from AI-controlled states is planned, including movement of their own transportation.

Trade Objects

Trade extends beyond basic resources and becomes part of strategic management:

  • raw materials and finished products;
  • vehicles and machinery produced by the player’s own industry;
  • vehicle blueprints and modular transport configurations;
  • production licenses;
  • territories and economic agreements (as diplomacy systems expand).

This creates a unified space where economy, industry, and technology become instruments of influence.

Tariffs and International Relations

Every trade operation is regulated through tariffs and diplomatic relations:

  • basic transactions are subject to tariffs;
  • improved relations reduce costs;
  • trade agreements optimize resource flows;
  • free trade agreements become possible.

As a result, diplomacy directly affects economic efficiency and access to external markets.

Integration with the Economy

Foreign trade is closely connected to other systems:

  • it compensates for resource shortages caused by limited extraction;
  • it allows economic specialization through imports and exports;
  • it affects logistics network load and infrastructure usage;
  • it supports early development before domestic production becomes sufficient.

Poor trade management can lead to import dependency or overloaded logistics networks.

Future of the System

The foreign trade system will continue to expand alongside diplomacy and state AI development:

  • dynamic country behavior and changing trade conditions;
  • the influence of ideology on available agreements and partners (v0.9);
  • more advanced economic and political treaties;
  • integration with military campaigns and territorial control (v0.6).

This will transform trade into a full geopolitical tool rather than a simple resource exchange mechanic.

Importance for the Player

In State Rise, trade is the continuation of the economy beyond national borders. It determines:

  • the speed of development and industrial scaling;
  • resilience against crises and shortages;
  • influence over other states;
  • access to technologies and resources.

A well-designed trade policy allows the economy to become an instrument of strategic dominance.

title: One Year of State Rise Development
preview: Looking back at the first year of development, sharing the story behind the project, and discussing plans for the future.
content:
Greetings!

State Rise recently celebrated its first anniversary, and we would like to take this opportunity to look back on what has been accomplished so far, as well as share some information about the project that we have never talked about before.

How the Idea Was Born

Let's begin with the origin of the project itself. One year ago, State Rise did not yet exist. The idea emerged long before the first line of code was written.

While playing Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic, I often found myself wishing the game would go beyond city-building and industrial planning. I wanted to see diplomacy, international politics, and the ability to test the strength of my own nation through military conflicts. At the same time, I wanted wars to have a direct impact on the country's development.

Later, I played Kaiserpunk, where I found something closer to what I had been looking for: the addition of wars and a global layer to the standard gameplay loop. However, in my opinion, this came at the cost of a fairly simple economic and logistics system. Then came Manor Lords. It was almost exactly what I wanted, but I hoped to see a similar concept set not in the medieval era, but in a more modern historical period, spanning from the end of the First World War to the later decades of the twentieth century.

At some point, I stopped waiting for someone else to create the strategy game I wanted to play. The idea was simple: combine city-building, economics, logistics, politics, diplomacy, and warfare into a single project and see how far it could go. That decision ultimately led to the beginning of work on State Rise.

First-Year Results

A tremendous amount of work has been completed over the past year. Nearly all of the planned gameplay systems that do not depend on artificial intelligence have already been implemented. A fully functional prototype has been created, and what it currently lacks most are high-quality models, textures, and interface design.

Production, transportation, population and economic simulation, and city construction systems are already fully operational. The foundation for modding support has been established, and the ability to add custom production buildings is currently being actively tested. The core game has been almost completely translated into six languages, although those translations still require verification by native speakers. Save and load functionality has also been implemented, and work on music and sound design has begun.

In addition, more than 20 development log posts have already been published, and a dedicated website has been created, where you are currently reading this article. One of the next planned steps is the creation of a YouTube channel that will feature patch overviews and showcases of the game's mechanics and features.

It is worth mentioning that all current development is being carried out by a single person, which makes community support especially important. Every mechanic, texture, sprite, sound effect, and development post has been created manually, with the exception of AI-generated images used at the very beginning of the project's journey. These were quickly replaced by actual in-game screenshots as soon as the game had even a minimal visual identity of its own.

Short-Term Plans

Version 0.6.3 is expected to be completed within the next few days. It already contains a reasonably playable build, although it still lacks the visual presentation originally planned for this stage. If community reception is positive enough, the first public free version will be released on the game's itch.io page.

Once this milestone is complete, full-scale implementation of scripted AI systems will begin. These systems will automate various processes and control neighboring countries, bringing significantly more life to the world. Further improvements to the visual side of the project are also planned in order to create a stronger first impression than the game currently provides.

Immediately after the current roadmap is completed, a Steam page will be created, followed by the game's release into Early Access.

Thank You for Your Support

Finally, I would like to thank every reader for their interest in the project. Development is ongoing, and your support helps me stay motivated and remain faithful to the original vision.

Thank you to everyone who follows the development of State Rise. Every comment, review, or even a simple view of a post helps demonstrate that the project is interesting not only to its developer.

There is still a great deal of work ahead, and the second year promises to be no less eventful than the first. We hope that expectations will be met and that the game will find its place among the many strategy titles available.

With love,
The Statecraft Bureau
